phrases.english_text: One time, there was a disagreement. We were in high school they kept us in a room, and they were calling us rink-a-dinks. The coach, his name was Mr. Ellis said we’ll play a game with them. We beat them real bad and they got mad. Mack Buzzard and Leon Hill. Where they jump for the tip off [center court]—they made them get in the circle and fight. And then the coach stopped the fight and asked if anybody else wanted to fight. phrases.english_text: Uksudi. He used to look for snake skin and used it for medicine. He said people from long ways off came to get medicine. Still, there are a lot of snakes around there. And Granny, when I was little, I had asthma and granny made medicine for me. I wish I paid attention to what she used. “What I’m fixing here, I’m going to add cream to it. Just eat a little bit every day,” she said. When I was doing that it, it didn’t bother me and then after a long while it came back. It was good and then Ayvl(i), ...okay... he was a true believer of his using tobacco, you know. I thought, “Oh gosh.”

phrases.english_text: I used to be there cause the girl worked there. I would go home about 10 o’clock, she would drop me off and they said she started running around. And when she takes Granny with her, “Let’s take her to Vian.” “Where are we going?” I said. “To somebody named Smith,” she said. “Why do you do what he says to do?” “Let’s just go over there,” she said. phrases.english_text: “I told you,” Granny said to him. I wasn’t saying anything and my aunt brought packs of Pall Mall cigarettes. I don’t know what the old man did with them but they were opened upside down when he brought them back. So, he told my aunt how I should smoke them, first the east –what's the name for ‘east?’-- smoke and blow in all [four] directions. He said, “Do not bring them in the house.” My aunt had a chicken house and that’s where she put them. I did that every day when I got up and I was sure getting tired of it after a while. At first, I just puffed a little bit and then later I went to really smoking it. And uh...boy about going on the 3rd week, I was sitting on the stump and I quit turning around.

phrases.english_text: “Now everybody’s going to get lazy!” she told me. She had water and a little cook stove. Granny was little, she 4’9. I would put water in a big pan and put it on top of the stove and when it got real hot, I put it on the table and washed the dishes. I would put them on the table and Louise was, the one I was taking care of, was drying the dishes. She wasn’t really bad off and Granny she really had them muscles. Her legs, arms, I think she was 82 when she died. She was strong, until she got the arthritis. That’s when she started hurting. “It’s hurting my arms,” she would say. And me, I’m getting crippled too, my hips are going out.

phrases.english_text: I think everybody should just speak their language at home and the kids will slowly pick it up. At home, that’s what they’re doing, I don’t really understand when they talk but at least they’re trying. Nan Usdi we raised her, and we always talked to her in Cherokee. When she was about three years old, she started talking Cherokee. “Ni!” she said one time when were heading to church. “There’s a cow!” she said. “What she say? What she say?” said her sisters. I told them, “She’s telling you that’s a cow she sees.” When she started school she didn’t talk—but when I talk to her she understands. I tell her to do something and she does it. I don’t know if she still knows, but I don’t have to say anything. She’ll do things at home. When she talks, it sounds pretty, cause she can make those sounds real well. I used to like to hear her talk.

phrases.english_text: Bad times. I grew up hearing my grandpa talk about it and it is happening now. A long time ago, 1970 he died. When he walked around outside looking for wood, I’d be walking right behind him. He would pray all the time, asking for everything to be alright and also he prayed for the grandkids. Just have them taken care of well, that’s what I would hear. He would sit down when he got to talk. “Real bad times are coming,” he would say. I don’t know if it’s God’s will why the kids are turning the way they are, they’re mean. All this stuff they’re using. Gina used to point out to me where Stephanie and them lived in Tahlequah. I’m just gonna tell you. I guess there was something in it, but they took the baby away from her. I stayed in Tahlequah for about three months, cause somebody had to stay there, they said. I was working at Baldore.

phrases.english_text: Mike’s aunt got there and would relieve me. That girl was kinda, sorta weird because she changed right away. “What’s going on with you?” I said to her. “Nothing.” She would be crawling on the floor listening to something. She was scaring the kids. So I didn’t want to, but I started praying. They brought her kids back to her. It was Memorial Weekend they had a fight, but I don’t know what happened. Then they took their kids away again. When they called me, they said they were taking the kids and I told them let me talk to her. So when I talked to them I told her I had gone through the same thing when I was young and I said, “Don’t do that to them. Tell their aunt to bring them over here.
